 KU rallies to beat WVU, 86-82, and advance to Players Era 8 championship
 By Henry Greenstein     Nov 18, 2026
 AP Photo/Abbie Parr 
 Kansas guard Tre White (3) shoots over West Virginia guard Seydou Traore, left, during the second half of an NCAA college basketball game in the Players Era tournament, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, in Las Vegas. 
 LAS VEGAS — The Kansas men’s basketball team rallied from an 11-point second-half deficit and escaped West Virginia, 86-82, in the semifinals of the Players Era 8 tournament on Wednesday night at Michelob Ultra Arena.
 “All games aren’t going to be pretty,” KU coach Bill Self said. “We played through foul trouble, we played without two starters, and we hung in there and did a really nice job.”
 Playing without Melvin Council Jr., who recently broke his foot, and Tyran Stokes — the star freshman was a game-time decision after suffering a bone bruise on Tuesday and remains day-to-day — the Jayhawks relied heavily on Tre White, who made a series of key free throws in the final minute and finished with 21 points to lead the Jayhawks. 
 “It was a great feeling,” White said. “I missed a couple (free throws) in a row, and I just had to smile, just take that pressure off, just kind of live in the moment. (Trey Kaufman-Renn) talking to me helped me stay in that center, stay in that moment and just knock it down.”
 Senior forward Keanu Dawes, who filled in for Stokes, recorded an 18-point, 12-rebound double-double, and Kaufman-Renn scored 19 with seven rebounds.
 WVU’s star freshman guard Miles Sadler tormented the Jayhawks all night and scored 34 points, but cooled off in the final minutes when KU was able to pull ahead. 
 “I’d say it was definitely a five-man job,” White said. “He’s so quick, three-level scorer. Kudos to him, he’s a great player, and tonight we definitely couldn’t guard him with one player. We got to take on that challenge a little bit better, and kudos to him, he made it hard for us tonight.”
 Martin Somerville made four 3s and scored 16 points for the Mountaineers, but they went 0-for-11 from beyond the arc in the second half.
 “Yesterday we came out and shot 85% for most of the game — come out this game, we miss a lot of shots, turnovers, all the wrong stuff, but we found a way, and great teams do that,” Kaufman-Renn said.
 Dawes and Kaufman-Renn scored twice in the opening minutes to help KU go ahead 13-9 by the under-16 timeout. However, the Jayhawks’ offense didn’t develop much of a rhythm early, and West Virginia used tight defense and a couple of 3s to narrow the gap, tying the game just inside the 12-minute mark when Somerville connected from the right wing.
 The Mountaineers then went ahead on a step-back 3 from Sadler. Kaufman-Renn responded with a spinning hook shot, but Somerville hit another to make it 23-21.
 WVU made six shots in a row, and the last, a driving layup by Sadler that brought him into double figures, was enough to prompt a timeout from Self with the Jayhawks down five.
 KU’s attempts to get back in the game were inhibited by poor free-throw shooting — after entering the night 337th in the country at 61.4%, it opened 3-for-9 — and foul trouble for Dawes and Kaufman-Renn.
 A strong sequence from White helped the Jayhawks back into contention. He made one shot through contact, drew an offensive foul while defending in the post and then banked in a contested shot that made it 28-27 in KU’s favor.
 With six minutes left in the first half, Taylen Kinney committed his third foul, putting KU in a bit of an uncomfortable ball-handling situation with Council out.
 The teams continued to trade blows down the stretch, with Amadou Seini contributing a couple of hard-fought layups inside for the Mountaineers. Most of all, though, KU had no answer for Sadler, who drove inside for a bucket before the Jayhawks committed a pair of turnovers and he knocked down a short jumper to make it 47-42.
 Self called timeout, but it didn’t do much to get his team headed in the right direction. KU did successfully defend a step-back 3 from Finley Bizjack just before the buzzer to keep its deficit at 49-44 entering the half.
 “I thought West Virginia was really good, and that was the best guard that first half I think we’ve played against in a long time,” Self said. “Sadler dominated us, and we couldn’t keep him in front of us.”
 KU went into the break having shot 1-for-5 from deep to WVU’s 6-for-17 and 13-for-21 at the free-throw line compared to WVU’s 9-for-9.
 As evidenced by the number of free throws attempted, both teams dealt with serious fouling issues in the first half. Three Jayhawks and seven Mountaineers picked up at least two fouls each in the first 20 minutes.
 Not much happened in the opening minutes of the second half other than WVU committing more fouls and Sadler continuing to score. After the under-16 timeout, he completed a three-point play that gave the Mountaineers what was then their largest lead at 58-49.
 But the run continued even after he subbed out, at least until KU ended a scoring drought of more than three minutes on a corner 3 by White.
 The Jayhawks trailed 68-58 when Trent Perry tipped in a putback off a pair of misses, and KU forced a couple of turnovers by Sadler that eventually led to a transition layup for Dawes. WVU coach Ross Hodge called timeout as his team still held a six-point lead.
 Sadler missed a couple of deep jumpers under improved defense from the Jayhawks. KU got back within two points at 70-68 on a second-chance straight-on 3 by Dawes; however, on the next possession he committed his fourth foul.
 After Dawes blocked Sadler with six minutes to go, White got down the court in transition and set up Blyden for a three-point play that put KU ahead for the first time in the second half. 
 Sadler continued to get to the free-throw line as WVU’s offense began to center on giving him the ball for the entirety of the shot clock. With 3:16 to go, the Mountaineers briefly took a two-possession lead on a transition dunk by Brenen Lorient, his first points of the game.
 Kinney swiped the ball from an unsuspecting Mountaineer and set up Dawes for a drive that resulted in the fifth foul by Mouhamed Sylla. He then made both free throws to tie the game again.
 With KU down 82-80 after a bucket by Lorient, Kaufman-Renn made 1 of 2 at the line. After Somerville came up short on a 3, White added two more free throws.
 Out of a timeout, WVU got Kinney switched onto Sadler, and Sadler pulled up for a step-back jumper, but it was short.
 “We started switching five and trying to crowd the floor, and we didn’t do a very good job of it, but down the stretch I think we did do a good job of crowding the floor and not pressuring him to the point — you know, we couldn’t stay in front of him,” Self said. “I don’t know anybody that could probably stay in front of that dude. So we backed off and played more contain, and I think our help defense was a little bit better.”
 White got the rebound and continued to connect from the free-throw line to make it 85-82. Bizjack missed a wild attempt from deep while guarded by two Jayhawks. Seini managed an offensive rebound, but threw it away trying to get back out to the perimeter.
 Kaufman-Renn, who had struggled at the line, made one final free throw to end the game.
 The Jayhawks will face No. 8 Houston on Thursday at 10 p.m. Central time in the tournament championship. The Cougars beat No. 1 Florida 86-76 on Wednesday.
 “Houston’s terrific,” Self said. “You don’t control Florida like Houston did today if they’re not terrific. They got different faces, but they got the same coach (Kelvin Sampson), and that coach stresses toughness and ‘game starts when the ball’s in the air’ better than anybody maybe in America. I think they’re really good. I mean, they’re a team that has a chance.”
 “The outside noise is going to try to big up or make games bigger than what it’s supposed to be, but for us it’s just another mission to stand on our principles, hopefully get this dub,” White added. “It’s going to be a war for sure.”
